title: Delay In Trial No Ground For Bail When Accused Has Criminal Antecedents, Previous Conviction: Supreme Court
case_name: CHANDER PAL v. RAHUL @ VIKRAM & ANR
summary: A mere delay in trial cannot be a ground to enlarge an accused on bail on the strength of his right to a speedy trial while overlooking his antecedents and previous conviction, observed the Supreme Court, while setting aside the bail granted to an accused who had been granted bail in a murder case on the strength of his right to a speedy trial, overlooking his antecedents and previous conviction in an attempt to murder case involving the same deceased person.

note.Facts: The accused was granted bail by the Punjab & Haryana High Court on the sole ground of delay in trial, while his criminal antecedents and a prior conviction for attempt to murder (S. 307 IPC) were concealed.
note.Issue: Whether a mere delay in trial justifies bail when the accused has antecedents and a previous serious conviction.
note.Held: The Supreme Court set aside the High Court’s bail order, cancelling the bail and directing the accused to surrender.
note.Principle: A delay in trial alone cannot be a ground for bail if the accused has criminal antecedents and a prior conviction; the court must balance the right to a speedy trial with societal interest.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – bail provisions; could be asked on the test of “balancing right to speedy trial vs. societal interest” and the requirement to consider antecedents and prior convictions when granting bail.

title: 'Stop Acting Like Bahubali': Supreme Court Chides Bihar Sessions Judge For Order Punishing SP For Contempt
summary: The Supreme Court today pulled up a Bihar Sessions Judge over the conviction of a senior police officer for contempt for non-compliance of the judge's directions. The top Court also questioned the Sessions Judge's understanding of the law and advised him to stop acting like a "Bahubali".

note.Facts: A Bihar Sessions Judge convicted the Rohtas Superintendent of Police for criminal contempt under Section 384 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (corresponding to Section 345 CrPC) for willfully disobeying the judge’s directions, imposing a fine of Re 1 and directing training reforms for IAS/IPS officers.
note.Issue: Whether the non-compliance of a police officer with a Sessions Judge’s direction amounts to a crime in the face of the court punishable as criminal contempt under Section 384 BNSS/Section 345 CrPC.
note.Held: The Supreme Court held that the Sessions Judge erred; a failure to comply with a direction does not constitute a “crime in the face of the Court” and the conviction was improper.
note.Principle: Non-compliance with a judicial direction is not criminal contempt unless the act is a direct affront to the dignity or authority of the court; contempt must involve a “crime in the face of the Court”.
note.Provisions: Section 384 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Section 345 CrPC, Article 227 Constitution (cited in discussion).
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – contempt of court; focus on the elements of criminal contempt (Section 345 CrPC) and the limits of a Sessions Judge’s contempt jurisdiction.

title: CJI-led Bench Of Supreme Court To Hear Umar Khalid, Sharjeel Imam Bail Pleas On Nov 25
summary: The Supreme Court is set to hear bail pleas of former JNU scholar Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the 2020 Delhi riots larger conspiracy case after the Delhi High Court denied them bail recently.

note.Facts: The Delhi High Court denied bail to former JNU scholar Umar Khalid and Sharjeel Imam in the 2020 Delhi riots conspiracy case, imposing a one-year embargo on bail and conditioning release on the completion of protected-witness examination.
note.Issue: Whether the one-year embargo and the protected-witness condition can be relaxed to grant bail to Khalid and Imam.
note.Held: The Supreme Court has scheduled a hearing of the bail appeals on 25 November; no decision has been rendered yet.
note.Principle: The Court will consider whether procedural conditions (embargo period, protected-witness examination) imposed on bail can be relaxed in view of prolonged incarceration.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – bail provisions and judicial discretion in imposing conditions; could be asked on the test for granting bail versus conditions of protected witnesses.

title: Grandson has no coparcenary right by birth in property that fell to his living father on partition: SC
summary: Supreme Court: In an appeal by a minor through his mother seeking half a share in land that his father had obtained under a compromise decree in a family partition and later sold, a Division Bench of Augustine George Masih and Sunita Agarwal , JJ. held that, in view of Section 8 , Hindu Succession.

note.Facts: The appellant (a minor) claimed a half-share in land that had been allotted to his father in a 1994 partition compromise and subsequently sold in 1997. He argued that, as the son of a coparcener, he became a coparcener by birth in his grandfather’s ancestral property.
note.Issue: Whether a grandson (son of a living coparcener) has a coparcenary right by birth in property that had already been partitioned and allotted to his father.
note.Held: The Supreme Court affirmed that under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 a son’s son is not a Class I heir and therefore acquires no right by birth in the grandfather’s property once it is partitioned. The father’s share became his exclusive property, held as a tenant in common, and the grandson’s claim was dismissed.
note.Principle: Upon partition, the allotted share passes to the heir in his individual capacity; the coparcenary does not continue, and a grandson has no coparcenary right by birth in that share.
note.Provisions: Section 8, Hindu Succession Act, 1956; Section 6 (pre-2005) HSA; Section 29-A, Hindu Succession (Tamil Nadu Amendment) Act, 1989 (not attracted). Cases cited: *CWT v. Chander Sen*; *Bhanwar Singh v. Puran*.
note.Exam angle: Test on the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 – focus on Section 8 (Class I heirs) and the effect of partition on coparcenary rights; could be asked as “whether a grandson becomes a coparcener by birth after a partition” or “impact of Section 8 on inheritance of partitioned property.”

title: Supreme Court Suspends Sentence Of Godhra Train Burning Convict On Medical Grounds
summary: A bench comprising Justice MM Sundresh and Justice PB Varale passed an order considering that Irfan suffers from serious cardiovascular disease. The State did not dispute the medical condition of the convict.

note.Facts: Irfan Siraj Pada, convicted in the 2002 Godhra train-burning case, has been in custody for over 17 years and suffers from serious cardiovascular disease.
note.Issue: Whether the Supreme Court may suspend his sentence and grant bail on medical grounds despite the conviction.
note.Held: The Supreme Court suspended Irfan’s sentence and granted bail, accepting his medical condition and long-term incarceration.
note.Principle: A conviction can be stayed and bail granted when the convict’s serious health condition and prolonged imprisonment justify relief, even after the appellate process.
note.Exam angle: Criminal Procedure Code – bail and suspension of sentence on medical grounds; could be asked to frame the issue of granting bail to convicts with serious illness after long imprisonment.

title: Supreme Court strikes down two UP laws denying pension benefits with respect to service before regularisation
summary: The Supreme Court has struck down the Uttar Pradesh Qualifying Service for Pension and Validation Act, 2021, and the Uttar Pradesh Entitlement to Pension and Validation Act, 2025, as unconstitutional. [ Uttar Pradesh Ground Water Department Non-Gazetted Employee Association (Regd.) & Anr. v.

note.Facts: The Uttar Pradesh Qualifying Service for Pension and Validation Act, 2021 and the Uttar Pradesh Entitlement to Pension and Validation Act, 2025 sought to exclude work-charged, temporary or daily-wage service rendered before regularisation from pension calculations; employees challenged the statutes as unconstitutional.
note.Issue: Whether a law can retrospectively deny pension benefits for service rendered before an employee’s regularisation, thereby overturning the Supreme Court’s earlier ruling in Prem Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh.
note.Held: The Supreme Court struck down both Acts as unconstitutional, holding that regularised employees cannot be denied pension benefits for their pre-regularisation service.
note.Principle: Once an employee is regularised under a valid scheme, the “birthmark” of the original non-regular appointment is erased; the employer cannot later deny vested retirement rights by retrospectively redefining eligibility, as such denial violates Articles 14, 16 and 21 of the Constitution.
note.Provisions: Articles 14, 16, 21 of the Constitution; Prem Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2019).
note.Exam angle: Test on the constitutional validity of pension-related statutes under Articles 14, 16, 21 (e.g., issue-framing on “class within a class” and the effect of regularisation on service credit).

note.Issue: Whether the FIR invoking Sections 192, 196(1), 353(2) and 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita can stand given the petitioner’s claim that the statements were academic and not intended to offend the Veerashaiva-Lingayat community.
note.Held: (Not stated in the source – the decision is pending).

title: Madras High Court Quashes FIR Over Critical Remarks Against CM Vijay For Giving Govt Jobs To Karur Tragedy Victims
case_name: Thirumurugan v. State of Tamil Nadu and Another
summary: The Madras High Court recently quashed a criminal case registered against a man for posting a video criticising CM Joseph Vijay's decision to give government jobs to families of victims who lost their lives during the Karur Stampede in September last year.

note.Facts: The petitioner posted a video harshly criticizing Chief Minister Joseph Vijay’s policy of giving government jobs to families of victims of the Karur stampede; a FIR was filed under Sections 352 and 353(2) of the BNS and the petitioner sought quash.
note.Issue: Whether the video constitutes an offence under Sections 352 or 353(2) of the BNS, or whether it is protected political speech.
note.Held: The Madras High Court quashed the FIR, holding that the ingredients of the alleged offences were not made out and continuation of the proceedings would be an abuse of process.
note.Principle: Purely political commentary, even if harsh, does not attract criminal liability under Sections 352 or 353(2) of the BNS absent incitement to violence, provocation, false information or promotion of enmity; such speech is protected unless it threatens public order.
note.Provisions: Sections 528, 352, 353(2) and 173(3) of the BNS (as cited in the judgment).

note.Facts: A practising advocate was alleged to have participated in a corrupt transaction; his role was limited to conveying a demand for illegal gratification.
note.Issue: Whether an advocate who merely communicates a demand, without independently soliciting, demanding or accepting gratification, can be charged under the Prevention of Corruption Act and under Section 120-B IPC for criminal conspiracy.
note.Held: The charges under the Prevention of Corruption Act were set aside, and the criminal conspiracy charge under Section 120-B IPC was quashed.
note.Principle: Mere presence in the chain of communication, without evidence of a meeting of minds or a common unlawful object, does not make a person a co-conspirator or liable under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
note.Provisions: Prevention of Corruption Act (specific sections not stated); Section 120-B, Indian Penal Code; *Balvinder Singh v State of Rajasthan*, 2026 LiveLaw (Raj) 491.
note.Exam angle: Questions may test the applicability of the Prevention of Corruption Act and Section 120-B IPC, focusing on the requirement of an independent demand/solicitation or a “meeting of minds” for conspiracy liability.
